strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-documented weakness of reconstruction-based MBRL (L2 loss dominated by background) and proposes a sensible remedy by leveraging frozen, pre-trained video object segmentation (Cutie) to obtain compact object features, avoiding the brittleness of unsupervised slot-attention approaches in visually complex scenes.

Evaluation is reasonably extensive: the full Atari 100k benchmark with 5 seeds, a new and genuinely challenging Hollow Knight boss-fighting testbed with a custom environment/action-space/reward design, plus Meta-world tasks for continuous control.

The ablation and analysis sections are thorough and honest: vector vs. mask representations (Figure 4), attention vs. MLP policies, number of annotation masks, robustness to segmentation failures (zeroing analysis), a qualitative check of representation completeness, and an explicit category-wise breakdown (Table 2) showing gains concentrate exactly where the hypothesis predicts.

The paper is unusually transparent about limitations (duplicated instances, background representation, few-shot supervision) and provides qualitative evidence (Appendix B, H) supporting the core claim that reconstruction losses miss key objects.
Reproducibility appears good: full hyperparameter tables, loss details, environment setup, and annotation examples are provided.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially plumbing a pre-trained VOS model's features into an existing world model (STORM). Similar two-stage ideas exist (FOCUS, semantic tracklets, MWM), and the architectural contribution (categorical VAEs + spatial-temporal transformer over object tokens) is a straightforward adaptation rather than a new insight or technique.

Aggregate Atari performance does not advance the state of the art: OC-STORM's mean HNS (134.8%) is below both the original STORM (122% in the paper's own table context and its published results) and DIAMOND (146%), and the median (43.8%) is essentially unchanged from STORM*. The main win is against a re-run, lighter-configured baseline (STORM*), which weakens comparability with published numbers.

The method requires human supervision: hand-annotated few-shot masks (6 per Atari game, 12 per boss) and a user-specified object count K per environment. This weakens the 'general agent' framing and makes the comparison to fully self-supervised baselines somewhat unfair in the direction favorable to the authors; the paper's justification ('telling the agent the rules') is reasonable but limits generality.

The Hollow Knight evaluation has confounds: it is compared only against the authors' own STORM rerun under a newly designed reward scheme (termination-on-hit) that the paper itself shows significantly improves performance (Figure 7); the object-centric contribution and the reward-shaping contribution are not fully disentangled, only 3 seeds are used, and comparison to prior HK work (Yang, 2023) is admittedly 'not necessarily fair'.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the central '18 of 26 tasks' claim, and with 5 seeds many Atari per-game differences may not be meaningful; the HNS figures also obscure the wide per-game variance visible in Table 1 (large losses on Hero, Gopher, Frostbite, BattleZone).

Computational cost of running Cutie during both training data collection and imagination is not quantified (FLOPs, wall-clock, decision latency), which matters for a method whose selling point is practical efficiency in complex environments.

Since OC-STORM always retains the full visual module, part of the reported gain may come from added model capacity rather than object-centricity per se; the category-level analysis partially addresses this but is based on the authors' own (unvalidated) taxonomy of games.

strengths: The idea of injecting pre-trained, frozen foundation vision model features (Cutie) into a transformer world model (STORM) is a sensible and timely integration, and the vector-based object representation vs. binary-mask ablation (Figure 4) is informative and directly addresses a weakness of prior work like FOCUS.

The Hollow Knight evaluation is a genuinely novel and visually complex testbed, with careful engineering details disclosed (custom wrapper, action space, reward design, Hyper-V setup), and the paper honestly reports where OC-STORM does not help (e.g., non-object-centric games in Table 2, Pure Vessel at 100k steps).

An unusually thorough set of ablations: number of annotation masks (App. E.2), attention-based vs. MLP policy (App. E.1), robustness to segmentation failure via feature zeroing (App. K), plus continuous-control validation on Meta-world (App. J).

Results are reasonably convincing on the paper's own terms: OC-STORM beats STORM* on 18/26 Atari tasks and achieves the best-known sample efficiency on several Hollow Knight bosses, with training curves and standard deviations provided.
weaknesses: The method requires substantial task-specific human priors: per-game/per-boss manual annotation of key objects (6 masks per Atari game, 12 per HK boss) and a hand-specified number of objects K per environment. This weakens the central framing of improving sample efficiency/generality — the baseline receives no such prior — and limits applicability to environments where decision-relevant objects can be identified in advance by a human expert.

Overall evidence of improvement is modest and partially unconvincing: Atari median HNS barely moves (42.5% vs 42.5% STORM* / 43.8% OC-STORM), and mean HNS (134.8%) remains below DreamerV3 (125% is close) and well below DIAMOND (146%). The headline '18 of 26 tasks' claim glosses over many games where differences are within noise.

The game categorization in Table 2 (object-representable vs. not) appears post-hoc and convenient: OC-STORM wins in one bucket and loses in the other, and no objective criterion or pre-registration for the grouping is given, raising cherry-picking concerns.

Statistical rigor is thin: 5 seeds for Atari and only 3 seeds for Hollow Knight, with no significance testing despite the small margins on many tasks; Hollow Knight has no established baseline and comparisons to prior work (Yang 2023) are admittedly 'not necessarily fair'.

Novelty is limited: the contribution is essentially a pipeline that plugs an existing VOS model (Cutie) into an existing world model (STORM) with standard DreamerV3-style training; the architectural pieces (categorical VAE, spatial-temporal transformer, prediction heads) are inherited. No new learning principle is proposed.

Important practical costs are not quantified: Cutie inference overhead per step (it processes high-resolution frames, e.g., 420x320 upscaled Atari observations, at 9-25 FPS), wall-clock time, and memory vs. STORM are absent, yet they are central to whether the 'efficiency' claim holds.

Key claims are asserted rather than demonstrated: 'Cutie generalizes well to out-of-domain inputs' and 'these features capture state and position' are supported by a single qualitative reconstruction on one game (Boxing) rather than quantitative probes across environments.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: a seemingly irrelevant reference (Hyper-V documentation cited in the references), typos ('Hollow Kight', 'INTERGRATION', 'COMPARISION'), and evaluation details (e.g., how Cutie's recursive memory interacts with imagined rollouts during policy training) that are underspecified.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: reconstruction-based MBRL world models can miss small, decision-relevant objects due to L2-dominated reconstruction losses; the object-centric pipeline directly targets this failure mode, and the appendix (Section B) provides convincing qualitative evidence that STORM's reconstructions lose key characters in Hollow Knight.

The proposed OC-STORM pipeline is sensible and well-described: frozen Cutie object features (compact vectors, consistent across frames) combined with raw visual input inside a STORM-style spatial-temporal transformer. The modular design allows clean ablations (object only, visual only, both).

Extensive and honest evaluation: Atari 100k with 5 seeds over 26 games, a new Hollow Knight boss-fighting environment with custom wrappers, action space, and reward design (carefully documented in Appendix D), plus Meta-world for continuous control. Comparisons include a re-run STORM* with matched configuration, which is the right baseline.

Thorough ablation and analysis section: vector vs. mask representations, attention-based vs. MLP policy, number of annotation masks (6-shot vs. 1-shot), robustness to simulated segmentation failures (zeroing probabilities), and qualitative validation that Cutie features encode position/state.

The paper is unusually candid about limitations (duplicated instances, background representation) with illustrative examples in Appendix H, and carefully caveats the Hollow Knight comparisons as not strictly fair. Reproducibility appears strong: hyperparameters, annotation examples, and implementation details (including the Cutie zero-vector fix) are provided.

Practical significance: demonstrating that off-the-shelf foundation vision models can be plugged into MBRL without fine-tuning, and achieving strong win rates on difficult Hollow Knight bosses (e.g., 100% on Hornet Protector, 48% on Mage Lord at 100k steps), is a meaningful step for object-centric RL in visually complex domains.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core contribution is an integration of an existing frozen video object segmentation model (Cutie) into an existing world model (STORM), following the same spirit as FOCUS (TrackingAnything + DreamerV2). The architectural changes on top of STORM are relatively small; no fundamentally new algorithmic component is introduced.

The method requires task-specific human priors: the number of objects K is hand-specified per environment, and 6-12 annotation masks per game/boss must be hand-drawn. While the authors defend this as 'informing the agent of the rules', it limits generality, introduces per-task engineering, and the comparison to annotation-free baselines (STORM, DreamerV3, DIAMOND) is not apples-to-apples in terms of supervision.

Atari 100k results are not state-of-the-art: OC-STORM achieves 134.8% HNS mean vs. DIAMOND's 146%, and the median improvement over STORM* is marginal (43.8% vs. 42.5%). The headline claim rests on 18/26 wins against STORM*, but no statistical significance testing (e.g., IQM with confidence intervals, rliable) is reported, and 5 seeds is on the low end for Atari 100k.

The game categorization in Table 2 (object-representable vs. not) is defined post-hoc by the authors and is partially subjective (e.g., classifying Breakout, Kangaroo, or Seaquest as fully object-representable), which risks confirming the intended conclusion; results should ideally be reported per-game with significance rather than via author-defined groups.

The Hollow Knight evaluation lacks established baselines: only the authors' own STORM re-run and a rough, admittedly unfair comparison with a model-free Rainbow implementation are provided. Since the environment, reward shaping (virtual termination on hit), action space, and FPS are all newly introduced, the 'best-known sample efficiency' claim on Hollow Knight bosses is hard to verify independently.

Computational overhead of running Cutie (a large frozen VOS model) online at decision time is never quantified — wall-clock time, GPU memory, and how this trades off against the claimed efficiency gains of compact object representations. This matters for the practical-value argument.

Some analyses are thin: the representation-completeness study (Section 5.1) uses only one game (Boxing) with a small dataset, and the Meta-world appendix uses only 4 tasks with unknown seeds and no variance reporting against MWM.

strengths: The paper presents a practical and timely integration of few-shot pretrained video segmentation models (Cutie, SAM2) into model-based RL, enabling object-centric representations in visually complex environments (Atari 100k, Hollow Knight, Meta-world) without privileged internal state access or heavy labeling.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 26 Atari games, six Hollow Knight boss fights, four Meta-world tasks, two backbones (STORM/DreamerV3), two segmentation models, and two representation types (vector vs. mask), with meaningful ablations (number of annotations, segmentation-failure robustness, attention vs. MLP policy, compute overhead, missing-object ablation).

Honest and transparent reporting: the appendix comparison against external MBRL methods (SPR, IRIS, TWM, DIAMOND, Delta-IRIS) openly shows OC-STORM is not the top HNS-mean method on Atari, and the limitations section candidly discusses duplicated instances and geometric-structure failure cases with illustrative examples.

The Hollow Knight testbed is a genuinely novel, visually complex benchmark contribution with a detailed environment/action-space/reward design and a new reward-shaping scheme justified by experiments.
The analysis of why Cutie features work better than SAM2 features, and why vector representations beat mask-based ones (FOCUS-style), provides useful insights for future OCRL work.
Good reproducibility signal: full hyperparameter table, model structure, loss functions, annotation examples, latency/compute tables, and a stated project page.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the method is largely a well-engineered combination of an existing world model (STORM/DreamerV3) with off-the-shelf segmentation foundation models; the architectural changes (object tokens + spatial-temporal attention, query-token reward head) are incremental rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Human annotation of 6-12 frames per game plus manually specifying the number and identity of objects (K per game) injects substantial task-specific prior knowledge, weakening the claim of general applicability; the paper's defense of this ('informing agents of task rules') is reasonable but limits the 'few-shot' framing.

On the standard Atari 100k benchmark, OC-STORM's HNS mean (134.8%) trails DIAMOND (145.9%) and Delta-IRIS (138.3%), and the median improvement over baselines is modest; gains are concentrated in the 'obj-detectable' subset, so the SOTA-efficiency claim needs qualification.

Statistical support is thin in places: only 5 seeds on Atari and 3 seeds on Hollow Knight, with no significance testing; several per-game results degrade vs. baselines (e.g., Freeway, Frostbite, DemonAttack), and Hollow Knight curves show large seed variance.

Direct external comparison for Hollow Knight is essentially absent (only a 'rough', admittedly unfair comparison against a community Rainbow implementation), so the Hollow Knight SOTA claim rests mainly on internal STORM comparison.

The paper only reports 26 of the 57 Atari 100k games; while the selection criterion is stated, a full-suite evaluation (or at least discussion of the remaining games) would strengthen the benchmark claims.

Segmentation models are run online during sampling with no discussion of potential train/test discrepancy from frozen perception, and the failure-handling (zeroing features via attention-guidance-mask heuristics) feels somewhat brittle and under-analyzed.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three domains (Atari 100k, Hollow Knight, Meta-world), two world-model backbones (STORM, DreamerV3), and two segmentation models (Cutie, SAM2), with several useful ablations (vector vs. mask representations, number of annotations, robustness to segmentation failures, computational overhead).

The Hollow Knight evaluation on complex, visually rich boss fights is a refreshing departure from the usual visually-simple benchmarks, and the paper honestly identifies failure modes (duplicated instances, geometric structures) with illustrative examples.

The core idea is practical and well-motivated: pretrained video segmentation models can supply compact object features with only a handful of annotations, avoiding the poor object discovery of unsupervised slot-based methods.
The paper is generally well written, with detailed appendices covering model structure, loss functions, environment configuration, and hyperparameters, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core contribution amounts to fusing pretrained segmentation features (Cutie/SAM2) into existing world models (STORM/DreamerV3) via a spatial-temporal transformer. The closest prior work, FOCUS, already combines a tracking-based segmentation model with a Dreamer-style world model; the delta is mainly the choice of representation (vector vs. mask) and backbone, which feels incremental.

The headline claim of 'state-of-the-art sample efficiency' is overstated. On Atari 100k, OC-STORM's HNS mean (134.8%) is below DIAMOND (145.9%) and ∆-IRIS (138.3%), and its HNS median (43.8%) is only marginally above STORM (42.5%) and DreamerV3 (42.6%)—differences that are likely within seed noise. No statistical significance testing (e.g., IQM with stratified bootstrap as in rliable) is provided.

Evaluation rigor is weak in places: only 5 seeds for Atari and only 3 seeds for Hollow Knight; improvements in Figure 2 are modest on several bosses (e.g., Mawlek is a tie, God Tamer is actually worse in win rate). Per-game wins and losses are mixed, and aggregate claims rest on small samples.

The Hollow Knight results are confounded: the authors change the reward structure (+1 on hit, virtual termination on damage), the action space (multi-binary keyboard), and frame rate relative to prior work (Yang, 2023; Sun, 2024), while acknowledging these are 'not strictly a fair comparison.' The improvement attributable to OC representations versus these design changes is unclear, even though Appendix E.5 attempts a legacy-reward ablation on only two bosses.

The method requires game-specific manual annotations of objects and hyperparameters K per environment (6 masks per Atari game, 12 per boss), which undercuts the claimed generality and 'minimal labeling' framing; the practical burden and sensitivity to annotation choices across games are not fully quantified.
The comparison to MWM on Meta-world uses numbers taken from the MWM paper under different setups/tasks, which is not a controlled comparison; only four arbitrarily selected tasks are used.

Several Atari games show degradation relative to the STORM baseline (e.g., Gopher, DemonAttack, Frostbite, Breakout with SAM2 variants), and the 'Obj-detectable vs. Otherwise' categorization is post-hoc, which risks cherry-picking a favorable narrative.

strengths: The core idea is practical and well-motivated: injecting few-shot object representations from pretrained video segmentation models (Cutie/SAM2) into a world model to redirect model capacity toward small, decision-critical objects, addressing a genuine failure mode of pixel-reconstruction MBRL (clearly illustrated in Figure 1).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 26 Atari 100k games with 5 seeds, a new challenging Hollow Knight boss-fight testbed, 4 Meta-world tasks, two backbones (STORM/DreamerV3), two segmentation models (Cutie/SAM2), and vector- vs mask-based representations (FOCUS-style), with a fair apples-to-apples ablation design.

Extensive and genuinely informative ablations: completeness of object features (reconstruction probe), robustness to segmentation failures via zeroing, impact of the number of annotations (1-shot vs 6-shot), missing-object ablations, attention- vs MLP-based policy, and a detailed computational overhead analysis (Tables 5-6).

Strong reported results: consistent HNS gains over STORM/DreamerV3 baselines on Atari (134.8% mean vs 114.2%), larger gains in the 'Obj-detectable' subgroup (186.2% vs 147.7%), and clear improvements on all six Hollow Knight bosses with only 3 seeds each, including a 400k run demonstrating the ceiling on Pure Vessel.

Honest and thorough treatment of limitations (duplicated instances, geometric structure), a careful analysis of why Cutie features outperform SAM2 features, and a detailed appendix (losses, hyperparameters, environment setup, annotation examples) supporting reproducibility; project page and evaluation videos are provided.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited: the method is primarily an engineering integration of existing components (frozen Cutie/SAM2 features fused into a DreamerV3/STORM-style world model with spatial-temporal attention). There is no new learning algorithm or theoretical insight, and the architecture follows established DreamerV3 machinery.

The approach requires manual, per-environment prior knowledge: the number and identity of objects (K) must be specified by the user, and 6-12 hand-annotated masks per game must be crafted. This reduces the claimed generality and makes the method closer to providing task-specific supervision than a general sample-efficiency solution.

On the standard Atari 100k benchmark, OC-STORM is not state-of-the-art against external methods (HNS mean 134.8% vs DIAMOND 145.9% and ∆-IRIS 138.3%; median 43.8% vs 59.4%), which weakens the 'state-of-the-art sample efficiency' claim in the abstract; the strongest claims rest on the self-constructed Hollow Knight benchmark where no independent baseline exists.

Hollow Knight evaluation is weak on external comparability: only 3 seeds, comparison limited to the authors' own STORM baseline under their custom reward scheme, wrappers, FPS, and charm configuration; the rough comparison with Yang (2023) is acknowledged as not strictly fair, so the 'state-of-the-art on Hollow Knight' claim is not strongly substantiated.

The 'Obj-detectable' vs 'Otherwise' categorization is somewhat post-hoc and determined by the authors' assessment of segmentation quality, which could bias the interpretation of subgroup results; per-game wins over the baseline are inconsistent (e.g., Amidar, Frostbite, PrivateEye, ChopperCommand degrade under some variants).

Some methodological details are underspecified in the main text (e.g., how object tokens interact with the dynamics predictor during imagination, handling of variable object counts) and must be reconstructed from the appendix; the reason the 0.5 Lrep coefficient is used, and its sensitivity, is not ablated.
